title: Laurel Canyon
full_review:
"Laurel Canyon" (Sony Classics) is a repellent drama about an uptight Harvard med-school grad who takes his straitlaced fiancee home to Los Angeles, where his hip, hedonistic mom initiates her into the epicurean joys of sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll.

Despite competent performances by Frances McDormand, Christian Bale and Alessandro Nivola, the film, by writer-director Lisa Cholodenko, espouses that most dubious of chestnuts -- that self-fulfillment hinges on jettisoning social convention and embracing libertinism.

Sam (Bale) is a young, handsome, though somewhat dull first-year resident, recently engaged to the beautiful and brainy Alex (Kate Beckinsale). They are a picture-postcard of idyllic, upwardly mobile, emotionally repressed, J. Crew love.

Having accepted a staff position at a Los Angeles psychiatric facility, Sam jets off with Alex to California, with stern admonitions from her conservative kin against becoming Scientologists -- or, worse, vegetarians. Against his better judgment, Sam agrees to move in temporarily with his mom until they find something more permanent.

Upon arrival, they are welcomed by Jane (McDormand), Sam's pot-smoking, free-loving mother, a famous record producer with a proclivity for shacking up with her musical proteges, regardless of gender. Her newest platinum-digging bauble is Ian (Nivola), a libidinous Brit rocker with a velvet voice and a predatory glance which immediately zeroes in on Alex. Sam still harbors a deep-seated resentment toward his mother for his unconventional upbringing, and remains wary of her attempts at hospitality.

Jane's sybaritic oasis on Laurel Canyon, a twisting stretch of real estate populated by arty types, represents to Alex everything missing in her cloistered life, namely an uninhibited licentiousness. At one point she sighs, "My dad is a puritan who reads Proust and wears tweed." One assumes dear old Dad's tweed seemed less square to her when he footed the bill for Harvard.

Predictably, she begins to abandon her studies and surrenders to the intoxicating, bohemian allure of Jane's entreaties. Alex soon finds herself frolicking in a pool with the reptilian Ian and locking lips with her sexually equal-opportunistic future mother-in-law. Meanwhile, Sam's fidelity is tested by the tempting advances of a ravishing co-worker, Sara (Natasha McElhone). Prompted by a pang of conscience, Jane pulls the plug on Ian and Alex's jam session, but not before Sam discovers their twisted secret tryst.

The moral vacuity that unfolds in the film could be pardoned if the characters actually learned from their mistakes, but after lamenting her indiscretions Alex actually thanks Ian for helping to "open her up." Sam on the other hand, still smitten with Sara, admits that he must sacrifice his true feelings for her in order to make it work with Alex. In the end no one is happy; happiness is not an option, just sublimation.

In one of the few emotionally honest scenes, Jane shares a cathartic poolside moment with Sam, where she expresses sincere regret over being such a failure as a mother. Her lifestyle has left her haggard and wracked with guilt, but there is no indication that her remorse will prod her to change her promiscuous ways.

Much of the narrative is mired by a discursive plot that meanders like Laurel Canyon Road itself, full of emotional cul-de-sacs which remain unresolved.

Yet far more disconcerting is the pervasive self-gratification, disguised as self-assertion, promoted throughout the film. The movie would have audiences believe that Alex will find the yellow brick road to personal fulfillment if she'd just relax, smoke a joint and exchange bodily fluids with her soon-to-be mother-in-law. This view -- liberation via libertinism -- has grown a bit long in the tooth. Its proponents have been singing the same tune since film critics wore bowler hats. Thankfully, this disagreeable film does little to bolster the attractiveness of their argument.

Due to sporadic sexual content, fleeting nudity, several instances of same-sex kissing, recurring recreational drug abuse, intermittent rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
